name: Gingivectomy

lead: Gingivectomy is a dental procedure in which part of the gum is cut away. Periodontists have used it for decades to remove overgrown tissue and reduce gum pockets, and in appearance circles it is used to shorten a gummy smile so more tooth and less gum shows.

A dentist or periodontist trims a strip of gum with a scalpel, electrosurgical unit or laser and lets it heal. Where the extra gum display comes from tissue overgrowth or delayed tooth eruption, trimming exposes more of the tooth crown. Dental sources describe up to about 3 mm of gum display when smiling as commonly considered typical. Research is substantial for gum disease and healing, with fewer, smaller studies on gummy-smile cases specifically.

paras: It is done in a dental chair under local anaesthetic after a diagnosis of what causes the gum display. When the cause is the jawbone, upper lip or tooth position, other procedures are usually discussed instead. Good plaque control afterwards matters.

Reported issues include pain for a few days, bleeding, slow healing, tissue regrowth if plaque control is poor, and recession that can open dark gaps called black triangles between teeth. Electrosurgery may cause more damage to neighbouring tissue than a scalpel. It is a clinician-performed procedure.

chain: Less gum showing in a smile
angle.text: Gingivectomy reshapes gum tissue to reduce a gummy smile or remove overgrown gums so more of the tooth shows. The change is visible once it heals, and the procedure is long established in dentistry.

lead: Gingivectomy is a dental surgical procedure in which part of the gum tissue (gingiva) is removed. It is described as the oldest surgical approach in periodontal (gum disease) therapy and is usually performed either for appearance or to improve the outlook for a tooth [1][2]. Common indications include suprabony periodontal pockets, enlarged gums (including drug-induced overgrowth), exposing more tooth for restorations, and reducing excessive gum display when smiling [1][1].

In looksmaxxing and cosmetic dentistry, gingivectomy is best known as gum contouring, the way people shorten the band of pink visible in a "gummy smile" and lengthen teeth that look short or square under a high gum line. Dental sources describe up to about 3 mm of gum display when smiling as commonly considered acceptable, with more than that classed as a gummy smile [2]. The effect is immediate once swelling settles: removing excess tissue exposes more of the crown that was already there [2][3].

Whether a gum-only procedure suits a given smile depends on the cause. Reviews group the causes of excess gum display into gingival (such as altered passive eruption or drug-related enlargement), skeletal (vertical excess of the upper jaw), muscular (an overactive upper lip) and anatomical (lip length, crown length or tooth position) factors, and each points to a different treatment [4][1]. Gingivectomy addresses the gingival group; lip- and jaw-driven cases are treated with other approaches such as botulinum toxin, lip repositioning or orthognathic surgery [5][4].

Clinical research on gingivectomy is substantial but mostly concerns periodontal disease, gingival enlargement and healing, including trials comparing scalpel and laser techniques and adjunct therapies such as low-level laser. Published studies of gummy-smile procedures specifically are fewer and smaller.

paras: The word gingivectomy literally means excision of gingiva. In clinical practice it covers a family of related soft-tissue procedures: classic pocket-reduction gingivectomy for periodontitis, gingivectomy for enlarged or overgrown gums, aesthetic gingivectomy (often with gingivoplasty, the reshaping of the gum contour) to even out or lift the gum line, and crown exposure ahead of restorations [2][6]. In consumer-facing material the aesthetic version is usually called gum contouring, and a periodontist or cosmetic dentist typically performs it [3].

The American Academy of Periodontology's then-president, Pamela McClain, told WebMD that contouring suits people whose teeth look short because gum tissue extends over the enamel, and that the tooth's underlying shape and size still determine how the finished smile looks [3]. Providers generally describe the visit as a single appointment under local anaesthetic, with more extensive anaesthesia if bone also has to be reshaped [3].

In a gingivectomy the clinician excises gum tissue to reduce pocket depth, reshape the gum line or expose tooth structure. It is described as the main historical treatment for reducing pocket depth in periodontitis, particularly suprabony pockets, where removing the pocket wall gives access for removing calculus [2].

Other indications include gingival enlargement, such as drug-induced overgrowth when severe, and hereditary gingival fibromatosis, where recurrence is described as unpredictable [2]. It can also expose sound tooth structure for restorative work when decay or fracture lies below the gum line [2][6].

Gingivectomy can also be paired with gingivoplasty, which reshapes the gum contour, as in the split-mouth laser study, so that the finished gum line looks natural around the teeth.[7] The appearance chain is direct: removing excess tissue exposes more of the crown, which shortens teeth that look stubby under a high gum line and reduces the band of pink visible when smiling.[2]

Dental references describe gum display of up to about 3 mm on smiling as commonly regarded as acceptable, and display beyond this as a gummy smile, which can be corrected by gingivectomy when tissue excess is the cause [2]. Conditions that need bone surgery, or where the pocket base extends beyond the mucogingival junction, are listed as contraindications, as are some aesthetic cases in the front of the upper jaw [2].

A registered trial has compared different periodontal plastic surgery techniques for gummy smile, and another compares digital with conventional guided gingivectomy for altered passive eruption [8][9].

A frequent soft-tissue cause of a gummy smile is altered (delayed) passive eruption, in which the gum margin sits too far down the crown after the teeth have finished erupting, so the teeth look short. A periodontal hygiene review cites a prevalence of about 12 percent in a study of more than 1,000 adults and describes it as underdiagnosed [10].

Under the Coslet classification, type 1 has a band of keratinised gingiva wider than 2 mm and type 2 has 2 mm or less; subcategory A has the bone crest 1.5 to 2 mm below the cemento-enamel junction, and subcategory B has it at or overlapping the junction [10]. The review says gingivectomy removes gum only, whereas crown lengthening removes gum and bone and is needed in subcategory B, where gingivectomy alone risks soft-tissue rebound [10]. Planning commonly uses bone sounding, surgical guides, mock-ups and digital smile design, and the review describes both digital and conventional approaches as effective [10].

Wikipedia's gummy smile article lists delayed passive eruption, an overactive upper-lip elevator muscle, excessive vertical growth of the maxilla and over-erupted upper front teeth as causes, alone or combined, and reports that the condition affects about 10 percent of US adults aged 20 to 30 and is more common in women [5]. A 2023 systematic review gives a prevalence range of 10 to 29 percent for increased gingival exposure [4].

Alternatives named in these sources include orthodontics, lip repositioning, orthognathic surgery, hyaluronic acid fillers and botulinum toxin injections into the lip muscles, which Wikipedia says last about six months [5][4]. Lip repositioning is noted in the 2023 review to recur within the first 6 to 8 weeks in some reports [4].

Gingivectomy and crown lengthening are often discussed together because both expose more tooth. Crown lengthening is a surgical procedure, usually performed by a periodontist, that exposes more tooth by removing gum tissue and supporting bone; it can also be done orthodontically by pulling the tooth into a higher position [11]. Wikipedia describes the aesthetic version as adjusting the gum-to-tooth proportions in a gummy smile and the functional version as improving crown retention or giving access to decay below the gum line [11].

The distinction rests on biologic width, the zone between the base of the gum pocket and the bone crest, averaging about 2 mm but ranging from roughly 0.75 to 4.3 mm in the literature summarised by Wikipedia [11]. Restorations or cuts that invade it are described as able to cause chronic inflammation, recession and bone loss, which is why clinicians assess bone position before deciding between a soft-tissue-only gingivectomy and bone-involving crown lengthening [11][10]. Wikipedia's gingivectomy article lists the need for bone surgery as a contraindication to gingivectomy [2]. The crown-lengthening article also says bone removed this way cannot easily be restored, which some clinicians weigh in implant planning [11].

sections.h: Gingival enlargement and other medical uses
paras: Outside cosmetics, a major use is removing overgrown gum. Wikipedia's gingival enlargement article reports that plaque-related inflammation is the most common cause, that drug-induced overgrowth is mainly linked to anticonvulsants such as phenytoin, calcium channel blockers and cyclosporine, and that surgical removal is used when a fibrotic component persists after scaling and root planing [12]. Changing the medication often resolves drug-related cases, and the 1985 CO2 laser report on phenytoin overgrowth is an early laser example [12][13].

The article on gingivectomy adds that surgery for drug-induced enlargement gave no recurrence in most patients after one year in one series, whereas in hereditary gingival fibromatosis recurrence is unpredictable and repeat procedures may be needed [2]. Registered trials compare scalpel and diode laser gingivectomy for gum overgrowth in orthodontic patients [14][15].

Scalpel gingivectomy is the traditional method. Electrosurgery uses high-frequency current to cut and coagulate; compared with a scalpel it gives a drier field and less postoperative pain but may cause more damage to adjacent tissue, slower healing and a stronger inflammatory response [2].

Lasers (Nd:YAG, CO2, diode) are also used. Proposed advantages include a bloodless field, minimal pain and no need for a surgical dressing, while animal studies have found that higher laser energy can cause scarring and delayed healing [2]. A CO2 laser report from 1985 described its use for removing phenytoin-related overgrowth [13].

Digital planning is an active area: a registered trial compares digitally guided with conventional gingivectomy for altered passive eruption, in which a printed guide marks how much tissue to remove [9][10]. Platelet-rich fibrin injections and topical gels are also being studied for healing after the procedure [16][17].

Healing is reported to depend heavily on plaque control; without good hygiene and follow-up, disease and tissue overgrowth are likely to return [2]. Discomfort usually subsides within a few days, and patients may find cleaning difficult at first, so professional cleanings are advised [2].

Reported undesired outcomes include gum recession leading to black triangles between teeth [2]. An experimental dog study from 1984 examined recession at sites with a narrow band of keratinized gingiva, which is why remaining attached gingiva is a consideration in case selection [18]. A survey of patient pain after different periodontal therapies has been published in the Journal of the American Dental Association [19].

Wikipedia's description of recovery after scalpel gingivectomy says patients avoid chewing on the site, rinse with an anti-plaque agent, have sutures removed later, use softened brushes and toothpicks during early healing with interdental brushes avoided, and are checked about every two weeks at first.[2] Electrosurgery is reported to reduce bleeding and post-operative pain, but it is not widely used because of cost and limited information, and laser healing evidence is mixed, with low energy settings favoured in animal studies.[2] Systemic health also influences outcomes.[2]

Because lip-driven gummy smiles are managed differently, much recent research on excessive gum display concerns non-gingivectomy approaches. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis in the Journal of Clinical Medicine, registered with PROSPERO, pooled 11 studies of botulinum toxin A for gingival smile: reductions in gum exposure averaged 3.22 mm at two weeks and 2.70 mm at three months, with high heterogeneity and most studies at moderate risk of bias; longer-term data showed a tendency toward recurrence [4].

For gingivectomy, the registered trial NCT05616715 compares periodontal plastic-surgery techniques for gummy smile and NCT05969132 compares digital and conventional guided gingivectomy [8][9]. Dental guidance that emphasises diagnosing the cause first is consistent across the sources, because a hypermobile lip or extra vertical jaw growth can look the same as excess gum on a photograph [4][10].

Recovery is described as a few days of soreness that usually subsides within a few days, with gums generally healing quickly after a contouring visit and longer when bone is reshaped [2][3]. Wikipedia lists post-operative care after scalpel gingivectomy as avoiding chewing on the site, rinsing with an anti-plaque agent, and follow-up checks about every two weeks at first [2].

Prices vary by country, number of teeth and method (scalpel or laser), and the clinic-published figures that circulate are marketing material rather than independent surveys. For that reason this article does not give a price. Results are described by providers as immediate once swelling subsides and generally lasting where plaque control is good, with regrowth reported when hygiene lapses [2][3].

Gum contouring appears in appearance communities as one of the 'hardmaxxing' or surgical options within the smile and teeth category, alongside veneers, whitening and orthodontics, because gum display changes how long the teeth look and how much of the smile is teeth versus gum. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article lists surgical and medical interventions as the 'hardmaxxing' end of the practice, and describes the broader scene as having grown from incel and manosphere forums and spread through TikTok and streamers in the 2020s [20].

Because the procedure is routine in dentistry and offered by general dentists, it is discussed less as a forum controversy and more as one step in a smile-design plan, usually discussed together with questions of who to see (periodontist or cosmetic dentist) and whether a second opinion on the cause of the gum display is needed.

Landmark 1970s trials in Journal of Clinical Periodontology compared gingivectomy with other periodontal surgical techniques, such as flap procedures, in patients with optimal and with poor plaque control, and followed healing for up to two years [21][22]. A 2016 review discussed scaling and root planing versus conservative surgery for chronic periodontitis [23]. A review on crown lengthening describes the surgical options for exposing tooth structure [6].

A 2008 split-mouth controlled pilot study in 20 patients reported improved wound healing when low-level laser irradiation was applied after gingivectomy and gingivoplasty [7]. Registered trials include comparisons of scalpel and diode laser gingivectomy in orthodontic patients with gum overgrowth, injectable platelet-rich fibrin after gingivectomy, and herbal or synthetic gels after gum surgery [14][15][16][17].

Wikipedia's gingivectomy article collects further studies: a 1976 retrospective comparison reported gingivectomy more successful than non-surgical treatment for pockets of 3 mm or deeper, a 1999 series found most drug-induced enlargement cases did not recur after a year, and reviews of electrosurgery describe a drier surgical field but more adjacent tissue damage than a scalpel [2].

Grokipedia credits the French dentist Pierre Fauchard with an early description in 1742 and says the term was coined by H.P. Pickerill in 1912, with the procedure developing in early 20th-century dental literature as a method of pocket elimination [1]. These details come from an AI-generated reference and have not been verified against primary sources here. Wikipedia describes it simply as the oldest surgical approach in periodontal therapy [2].

Wikipedia's article on Pierre Fauchard (1679 to 1761), whose 1728 Le Chirurgien Dentiste is widely called the first complete scientific description of dentistry, covers periodontal disease but does not itself describe a gingivectomy, so the Grokipedia attribution is reported here as that reference's claim only [24]. Wikipedia describes gingivectomy only as the oldest surgical approach in periodontal therapy [2]. Aesthetic use grew with the rise of cosmetic dentistry and later laser dentistry, and with the 1970s and 1980s trial literature that compared gingivectomy with flap procedures [21][22][13].

lore.intro: Gum contouring is promoted mainly by dental practices and cosmetic-dentistry guides, and discussed by patients and appearance communities as a way to fix a gummy smile; the claims below are the ones that recur in that coverage [3].

claims.claim: Gum contouring permanently fixes a gummy smile
Any gummy smile can be fixed by trimming the gums
Laser contouring is bloodless and nearly painless, so healing is quicker than with a scalpel
Botulinum toxin is a reversible alternative for a lip-driven gummy smile
Removing gum can leave gaps or sensitivity
